\cpara{The theoretical core: punishing defectors can sustain cooperation, but punishing those who fail to punish can lock an equilibrium in place, even one harmful to everyone. Boyd and Richerson's model (1992) supports the point: strategies that punish ``those who do not punish noncooperators'' can be stable, and ``can cause any individually costly behavior to be evolutionarily stable, whether or not it creates a group benefit.''}
\cpara{Two more cases from the author's circle, Robin Hanson and Michael Vassar, and the slogan ``Tolerate tolerance!''}

\cpara{Admits the annoyance and guesses, with ``I suspect'' and ``I wouldn't be surprised,'' that it is common and perhaps universal. The ``obvious evolutionary rationale'' is left unstated; presumably it is the enforcement of cooperation described two paragraphs earlier.}
\cpara{States the author's resolution: tolerate the more tolerant, and judge people only for their own mistakes.}

\cfact{``Inconsistently'' is asserted without argument. The best-known statement of the view is Karl Popper's ``paradox of tolerance'' (1945), which presents it as a limit tolerance needs in order to survive: ``Unlimited tolerance must lead to the disappearance of tolerance'' (as quoted in Wikipedia, ``Paradox of tolerance'').}
\cpara{Adds that a group that demands you hate the right enemies may be the wrong group.}
\cpara{Applies the rule once more: do not demand that friends be equally hostile to such a group.}
